rejected.title: Psychological factors in specific phobia
card: Classical conditioning
A phobia can be learned when a neutral stimulus is paired with something that already causes fear. The neutral stimulus then triggers fear by itself, and it becomes the conditioned stimulus.
Operant conditioning
A phobia can be kept going by negative reinforcement. Avoiding the feared thing brings relief, which makes the person more likely to avoid it again.
Catastrophic thinking
This means expecting the worst outcome and believing it is very likely. It makes the feared thing seem more dangerous than it is, so fear stays high.
Avoidance also stops the person from finding out that the feared thing may be harmless. This helps the fear last.
rejected.remember: Conditioning can build a phobia, relief from avoiding can keep it, and catastrophic thinking feeds it.

a.q: Tom was bitten by a dog and now feels intense fear at the sight of any dog. In classical conditioning, what is the sight of a dog now?
a.why: The sight of a dog was neutral before the bite. It was paired with the bite, so it now triggers fear by itself and is the conditioned stimulus. The bite was the unconditioned stimulus, and the fear is the response.
a.clue: Which stimulus was neutral before the pairing?

b.q: Priya fears lifts. She takes the stairs to her office on the ninth floor and feels relief each time. Which process is most likely helping her phobia continue?
b.why: Taking the stairs removes the fear of the lift, and this relief makes avoiding lifts more likely again. That is negative reinforcement, a form of operant conditioning. It is not positive reinforcement, because nothing pleasant is added.
b.clue: What does Priya get after avoiding the lift?

a.q: Ana got stuck in a lift during a blackout and was terrified. Now the sight of any lift makes her afraid. In classical conditioning terms, what is a lift now?
a.why: Before the blackout a lift was neutral. Paired with the frightening event, it now triggers fear on its own, so it is a conditioned stimulus. Being trapped in the dark was the unconditioned stimulus, and the fear is the response.
a.clue: Was a lift frightening before that day?

b.q: Josh fears dogs. When he sees one, he is sure it will attack and badly hurt him, so he crosses the street and feels relief. Which part best shows catastrophic thinking?
opts: Being sure the dog will attack and badly hurt him
Crossing the street to get away from the dog
Feeling relief once he is on the other side
Noticing the dog from far down the street
b.why: Catastrophic thinking is expecting the worst and believing it is likely, as Josh does when he is sure he will be badly hurt. Crossing the street and the relief after it are avoidance and negative reinforcement, which keep the phobia going.
b.clue: Which part is a thought about what will happen?

b.best: Being sure the dog will attack and badly hurt him

a.q: Ana got stuck in a lift during a blackout and was terrified. Now the sight of any lift makes her afraid. In classical conditioning terms, what is a lift now?
a.why: Before the blackout a lift was neutral. Paired with the frightening event, it now triggers fear on its own, so it is a conditioned stimulus. Being trapped in the dark was the unconditioned stimulus, and the fear is the response.

b.q: Josh has a phobia of dogs. Which of these best shows catastrophic thinking by Josh?
opts: Expecting any dog he passes to maul him
Crossing the road each time he sees a dog
Feeling relieved once a dog is out of sight
Getting a racing heart when a dog barks
b.why: Catastrophic thinking is a thought: expecting the worst outcome and believing it is very likely, such as being mauled by any dog. Crossing the road is avoidance, and the relief after it is negative reinforcement. Both keep the phobia going, but neither is a thought about what will happen.
b.clue: Look for the option that is a belief about the future.
